# Overview

This mini-project creates and maintains a `date_table` in PostgreSQL, providing a canonical calendar dimension for reporting.

# Setup

Ensure `DATABASE_URL` is available in the repository `.env` file.

```bash
pip install -r create-date-table/requirements.txt
```

# Run

From the repository root:

```bash
python create-date-table/create_date_table.py
```

# Table schema

One row per calendar day, keyed on `calendar_date`:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| `calendar_date` | The date (primary key) |
| `year`, `quarter`, `month`, `day` | Calendar parts |
| `month_name`, `day_name` | English names, e.g. `October`, `Wednesday` |
| `day_of_week` | ISO day number, Monday = 1 … Sunday = 7 |
| `weekday` | Monday = 0 … Sunday = 6 |
| `is_weekend`, `is_month_start`, `is_month_end` | Boolean flags |
| `week_num`, `iso_week`, `iso_year` | ISO week and ISO week-year (`week_num` equals `iso_week`; kept for the Power BI model) |
| `year_month`, `year_quarter` | Labels such as `2026-10` and `2026-Q4` |

# Notes

The script stages the rows in a temporary table and upserts them on `calendar_date`, so it is idempotent: new dates are inserted, changed rows are corrected and identical rows are left alone. After each scheduled run, a check fails the workflow if the table has gaps or does not cover 1 January 2025 to 31 December of next year. Seven fact tables (FX rates, FX Prime Brokerage, Treasury Simulator) reference it through foreign keys.

# Preview: calendar rows

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display

# Quarto runs from the project folder; a manual run may start at the repo root.
candidates = [Path('data/date_table.csv'), Path('create-date-table/data/date_table.csv')]
p = next((c for c in candidates if c.exists()), candidates[0])
if p.exists():
    df = pd.read_csv(p, parse_dates=['calendar_date'])
    print(f"{len(df)} rows from {df['calendar_date'].min():%Y-%m-%d} to {df['calendar_date'].max():%Y-%m-%d}")
else:
    print('No date_table.csv present; creating a small sample for demonstration:')
    dates = pd.date_range(start='2026-07-25', periods=7, freq='D')
    df = pd.DataFrame({'calendar_date': dates, 'year': dates.year, 'is_weekend': dates.dayofweek >= 5})
display(df.head(10))
```

```{python}
# Visual: weekdays vs weekend days per year
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
counts = (
    df.assign(day_type=df['is_weekend'].map({False: 'Weekday', True: 'Weekend'}))
      .groupby([df['calendar_date'].dt.year, 'day_type']).size()
      .unstack(fill_value=0)
)
counts.plot(kind='bar', stacked=True, figsize=(6, 3))
plt.title('Days per year' if p.exists() else 'Days per year (sample)')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Days')
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.legend(title=None, loc='upper left', bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1), frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
